title: Air India Is Slashing 145 International Flights a Week — and the Diaspora's Summer Plans Are the First Casualty
excerpt: A 27 per cent cut to international routes between June and August leaves millions of overseas Indians scrambling for alternatives during peak travel season
body:
For millions of Indians living abroad, summer is homecoming season. It is the time of family weddings, temple visits, and overloaded suitcases stuffed with gifts. But this year, the journey home just got harder — and more expensive.

## The Cuts

Air India, the Tata Group-controlled flag carrier, has announced it will slash approximately 145 weekly international flights between June and August 2026. The reduction amounts to a staggering 27 per cent of its international network, the deepest seasonal cutback in the airline's post-privatisation history.

The routes affected read like a diaspora directory. Delhi–Chicago: suspended entirely. Mumbai–New York JFK: reduced from daily to four times weekly. Delhi–San Francisco: cut to three weekly flights. Delhi–Vancouver: suspended. Services to Toronto have been trimmed by 35 per cent. European routes to Paris, Rome, Milan, Copenhagen, Vienna, and Zurich are all seeing frequency reductions. Even Tel Aviv, a route serving India's growing Israel corridor, remains halted.

Air India says it will maintain over 1,200 monthly international flights — but for passengers on affected routes, that statistic offers cold comfort.

## Context & Background

The airline's hand has been forced by a brutal convergence of factors. Jet fuel prices have surged roughly 130 per cent since the escalation of the West Asia crisis, with Aviation Turbine Fuel now accounting for approximately 40 per cent of Air India's operating costs. Pakistan's continued airspace restrictions — a consequence of the Iran conflict's regional spillover — have added flight time and fuel burn to every westbound route. And the broader geopolitical turbulence has driven insurance and overflight charges sharply upward.

Air India reported losses exceeding ₹26,700 crore (roughly $3.2 billion) for FY2025–26. Negotiations with oil marketing companies over relief on fuel pricing have stalled. The airline has also quietly terminated over 1,000 employees, citing operational restructuring.

None of this is occurring in a vacuum. India's wholesale price inflation hit a 42-month high of 8.3 per cent in April, driven largely by a 24.71 per cent spike in fuel and power costs. The rupee has depreciated 8.5 per cent against the dollar. For an airline that earns in rupees but pays for fuel and leases in dollars, the arithmetic is punishing.

## Current Developments

Passengers are scrambling. Social media is thick with complaints about cancelled bookings, limited rebooking options, and soaring fares on the routes that remain. A viral claim that Air India had cancelled "all" international flights until July was debunked — the actual impact covers 10–12 per cent of its global network — but the panic spoke to real anxiety.

Rival carriers sense opportunity. IndiGo, which recently ordered 30 Airbus A350 widebodies for long-haul expansion, is positioning itself to absorb displaced demand. Emirates and Qatar Airways, operating from hubs with cheaper fuel access, have increased capacity on India routes.

Yet for the diaspora, substitutes are imperfect. Air India's nonstop services to secondary American cities like Chicago and San Francisco have no direct alternatives. Connecting through the Gulf adds hours and uncertainty.

## Diaspora Impact

The timing is particularly cruel. June through August is peak season for diaspora travel — school holidays in North America, wedding season in India, and the annual pilgrimage of grandparents crossing oceans to meet newborns. Fares on surviving routes have already risen 25–40 per cent for the summer window, pricing out families who planned trips months ago.

For the roughly 4.5 million Indian passport holders in the United States and Canada alone, Air India has historically been more than an airline. It is the carrier that serves dal and rice at 35,000 feet, the one whose cabin crew speaks your mother tongue, the airline that tolerates three checked bags because it understands what going home means. Its retreat from key routes feels less like a scheduling adjustment and more like the severing of an umbilical cord.

## What's Next

Air India has characterised the cuts as temporary, tied to the summer fuel spike. But analysts are sceptical. If crude remains above $100 per barrel — and the West Asia situation shows no sign of resolution — the "temporary" could become structural. The airline's ambitious fleet modernisation, including new Airbus A350s and Boeing 787 Dreamliners, was predicated on expanding its international network, not shrinking it.

The Tata Group's turnaround plan for Air India was always going to be a multi-year slog. But the question the diaspora is now asking is simpler and more personal: when the airline they grew up with cannot afford to fly them home, who will?
